register.name: Medical emergency
register.frequency_sentence: Nearly every household like yours will have someone need emergency care in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Far from emergency care
sub_causes.note: Ambulances take about twice as long to reach rural homes (a median of about 14 minutes against 7).

sub_causes.name: Falls
sub_causes.note: Falls are a leading reason older adults need emergency care; clear floors and light the way at night.

register.name: Strong wind
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 95 (59 to nearly all) will lose power or have damage in a windstorm in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Derecho
sub_causes.note: A fast line of storms with hurricane-force gusts over hundreds of miles; outages can last days. Counted in the windstorm rate.

register.name: Phone or internet outage
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 95 (63 to nearly all) will lose phone and internet service for hours in a network outage in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: GPS or radio disruption
sub_causes.note: Space weather or jamming can degrade navigation and timing. Keep a paper map for the way home.

register.name: Wildfire
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 88 (38 to nearly all) will have to leave home or lose power because of a wildfire in the next ten years.

register.name: Supply chain disruption
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 86 (63–98) will find store shelves empty of things they need in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Fuel shortage
sub_causes.note: Gas stations run dry for days (the Colonial Pipeline shutdown, May 2021, and before hurricanes). It matters most with a generator or a long drive.

sub_causes.name: Cut off: an island or a single road
sub_causes.note: A bridge, ferry or the only road closes and the community is cut off for days. Plan for longer if that is you.

register.name: Hurricane
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 78 (62–91) will lose power or have damage from a hurricane or tropical storm in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Inland flooding from a tropical storm
sub_causes.note: A weakening hurricane can drop a foot or more of rain far inland (Helene in western North Carolina, 2024), cutting water service for weeks.

register.name: Stranded in a vehicle
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 78 (39–98) will be stranded away from home by a crash, breakdown or shutdown in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Black ice or dense fog
sub_causes.note: Chain-reaction crashes and closed highways. Counted in the stranding rate.

sub_causes.name: Transit shutdown or strike
sub_causes.note: Buses and trains stop and commuters without a car are stuck. Counted for commuters who travel by transit.

register.name: Job loss
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 77 (64–91) will have someone lose a job in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Livestock or poultry disease
sub_causes.note: An animal-disease outbreak (bird flu in dairy or poultry) can hit a farm's income.

sub_causes.name: Recession layoffs
sub_causes.note: Layoffs cluster in downturns; the high end of the job-loss range is a recession year.

register.name: Medicine shortage
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 71 (39–98) will have a daily medicine they cannot fill for days or weeks because of a shortage in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Hospital supply shock
sub_causes.note: A key hospital supply runs short (IV fluids in 2024, after Hurricane Helene closed a plant that makes a large share of the country's supply) and planned care is delayed.

register.name: Heat wave
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 63 will go through a heat wave in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: A blackout during a heat wave
sub_causes.note: When the power fails in extreme heat, air conditioning fails for everyone at once. It is the most dangerous combination; where it matters most it is a named scenario.

register.name: Flooding from rivers or heavy rain
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 58 (44–72) will have flood water reach their home in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Flash flood
sub_causes.note: Water rises in minutes on roads and near creeks; most flood deaths are people driving into it. Counted in the flood rate; turn around, don't drown.

sub_causes.name: Basement or street flooding in heavy rain
sub_causes.note: Drains overflow and water or sewage comes up into basements outside the mapped flood zone. It is the outside-the-zone part of the flood rate, higher with a basement.

sub_causes.name: Levee failure or overtopping
sub_causes.note: Counted on the dam and levee card, not here: leveed land is mapped outside the high-risk flood zone.

register.name: Wildfire smoke
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 44 (22–72) will go through days of unhealthy wildfire smoke in the next ten years.

register.name: Cold wave
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 28 will go through a spell of dangerous cold in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Rolling blackouts in extreme cold
sub_causes.note: Gas supply and power plants fail in deep cold and the grid cuts power in rotation or for days (Texas, February 2021). Already in the county's outage record.

register.name: Drought
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 19 (6–46) will have their well run low in a drought in the next ten years.

register.name: Long illness in the household
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 18 (10–45) will have someone sick at home for weeks in the next ten years.

register.name: Cyberattack on services
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 18 (7–39) will lose pharmacy, payment or other services to a computer outage or cyberattack in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Critical software failure
sub_causes.note: A faulty update or cloud outage takes down hospital, airline, bank or 911 systems for a day or more (July 2024). Counted in this rate.

sub_causes.name: Card or bank payment outage
sub_causes.note: Cards, bank apps or cash machines stop for hours to days. Keep some cash in small bills.

register.name: A household member is arrested or detained
register.frequency_sentence: For households with people the ages of yours, about 2 in 100 have someone arrested in a year, going by what people tell a national survey (2022–2024); police records suggest up to about 4 in 100. People arrested once are often arrested again, so over ten years fewer households are affected than a year-by-year count suggests. This counts arrests, not guilt or convictions.

register.name: Lightning
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 15 (4–43) will have lightning damage their home or cut their power in the next ten years.

register.name: Burst pipe or water leak
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 14 will have a burst pipe or leak flood part of the home in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Sewer backup
sub_causes.note: Sewage backs up through basement drains; standard home policies leave it out unless you add sewer-backup cover.

register.name: Ice storm
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 12 (4–36) will lose power or be stuck at home in an ice storm in the next ten years.

register.name: Chemical spill or release
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 12 (4–30) will be told not to drink the tap water, or to stay inside, after a chemical spill in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Release from a chemical plant
sub_causes.note: A plant that uses large amounts of toxic or flammable chemicals has a release or explosion (West, Texas, 2013). Counted in the chemical-release rate.

sub_causes.name: Train derailment with chemicals
sub_causes.note: A train carrying chemicals derails and burns or leaks; homes within a mile or two are evacuated (East Palestine, 2023).

sub_causes.name: Tanker truck spill
sub_causes.note: A tanker crash closes roads and may bring an order to stay inside nearby.

sub_causes.name: Pipeline rupture
sub_causes.note: A gas or oil transmission pipeline ruptures and burns or spills; nearby homes are evacuated.

sub_causes.name: Refinery, tank farm or port fire
sub_causes.note: A large industrial fire brings orders to stay inside and smoke for days.

sub_causes.name: Chemical spill into the water supply
sub_causes.note: A spill upstream of a water intake brings a do-not-use order for days (Elk River, West Virginia, 2014). Counted in the chemical-release rate.

register.name: Pandemic
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 11 (3–23) will live through a pandemic that changes daily life in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Mosquito- or tick-borne outbreak
sub_causes.note: Local dengue or West Nile spread brings spraying and advisories.

sub_causes.name: Local disease outbreak
sub_causes.note: Measles, hepatitis A or Legionnaires' in the community keeps people out of school or work. Check your vaccinations.

sub_causes.name: Bird flu (H5N1)
sub_causes.note: A candidate pandemic strain that so far passes from animals to people, not between people.

register.name: Break-in
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 10 (5–18) will have a break-in in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Identity theft and disaster scams
sub_causes.note: Accounts opened in your name, or fake contractors and FEMA impostors after a disaster. A credit freeze is free.

register.name: Local water or gas outage
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 10 (3–26) will have a gas leak or other local utility problem in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Toxic algae in the water supply
sub_causes.note: Algae toxins reach the treatment plant and a do-not-drink order follows (Toledo, 2014). Counted in the water-notice rate.

sub_causes.name: Gas main over-pressure or leak
sub_causes.note: Gas mains over-pressure or leak and homes must be evacuated (Merrimack Valley, 2018). If you smell gas, leave first, then call.

sub_causes.name: Water system failure for weeks
sub_causes.note: A treatment plant or system fails for weeks (Jackson, Mississippi, 2022; Asheville, 2024). The water targets use the county's drinking-water violations to size it.

sub_causes.name: Sewer failure
sub_causes.note: Pumps stop or mains break and toilets cannot be flushed. The sanitation supplies follow the water target.

register.name: Coastal flooding
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 9 will have coastal flooding reach their home in the next ten years.

register.name: Death or disability of an earner
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 9 (5–14) will lose an earner's income to death or disability in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Death in the family
sub_causes.note: A family member who does not earn dies: funeral costs and time off work.

register.name: Civil unrest
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 6 (2–15) will live under a curfew because of unrest in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Unrest around elections
sub_causes.note: Protests, clashes or curfews around elections or political events.

register.name: Regional blackout
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 5 (1–14) will lose power in a regional blackout that is not caused by weather in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Attack on power substations
sub_causes.note: Gunfire or sabotage at substations can cut power to a county for days (Moore County, North Carolina, 2022). Utilities report about 78 cases of attack, vandalism or theft a year, most with no outage (2019–2023).

sub_causes.name: Cyberattack on the grid
sub_causes.note: Hackers switched off parts of Ukraine's grid in 2015; no US case has cut power. Utilities report about 7 cyber events a year (2019–2023).

register.name: Winter storm
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 3 (1–10) will be snowed in or lose power in a winter storm in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Blizzard or lake-effect snow
sub_causes.note: Whiteouts or very deep snow close roads for days. Counted in the winter-storm rate.

sub_causes.name: Roof damage under snow
sub_causes.note: Heavy snow or ice loads a roof until it sags or fails. Counted in the winter-storm rate; clear flat roofs early.

register.name: House fire
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 3 will have a house fire in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Carbon monoxide poisoning
sub_causes.note: Carbon monoxide from a furnace, generator or car builds up indoors, most often after storms when generators run too close to the house. Shown beside fires, not added to them; a CO alarm is the defence.

sub_causes.name: Lithium battery fire
sub_causes.note: E-bike, scooter and power-bank batteries can catch fire while charging; charge them where you can see them.

register.name: Tornado
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 2 (1–6) will have a tornado damage or cut off their neighborhood in the next ten years.

register.name: Hail
register.frequency_sentence: About 8 (3–17) in 1,000 households like yours will have hail damage their home or car in the next ten years.

register.name: Earthquake
register.frequency_sentence: About 1 in 1,000 households like yours will feel an earthquake strong enough to knock things off shelves in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Liquefaction
sub_causes.note: Wet, sandy ground turns to slurry in strong shaking; pipes and foundations fail. Water outages last longer where it happens.

sub_causes.name: Fire after an earthquake
sub_causes.note: Broken gas lines and low water pressure let fires spread after a big earthquake. Know how to shut off the gas, and leave it to the gas company to turn it back on.

register.name: Financial crisis with bank closures
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 200 and 1 in 11 households like yours would have banks close for three days or more in a financial crisis in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Your own bank fails
sub_causes.note: Insured deposits (up to $250,000 per person at each bank) move to another bank, usually within days. The FDIC counts about 23 failures a year (2001–2025), most of them small banks.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a pandemic that changes daily life (about 11 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: Cards and bank transfers stop for days.
register.what_it_changes: Keep some cash in small bills (already in your plan) and a second account at another bank (free).

register.name: Very large volcanic eruption
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 130 and 1 in 26 households like yours would live through a year or two of higher food prices after a very large eruption somewhere in the world in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: A Yellowstone super-eruption
sub_causes.note: Devastation nearby and ash across much of the country. The USGS puts it at about 1 in 730,000 a year.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a regional blackout (about 5 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: A year or two of higher food prices and some shortages.

register.name: Severe pandemic
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 200 and 1 in 21 households like yours would live through a pandemic far deadlier than COVID-19 in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: A natural pandemic as deadly as 1918
sub_causes.note: The 1918 flu killed about 675,000 Americans. Records of pandemics over four centuries give the chance.

sub_causes.name: An engineered germ
sub_causes.note: A germ made or changed on purpose. There is no record to count; it is part of the expert range.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a curfew (about 6 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: Months of disruption, strained hospitals and lost income.
register.what_it_changes: Nothing new: the pandemic row already sizes your food and medicine.

register.name: War with attacks on US infrastructure
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 830 and 1 in 42 households like yours would lose power, water or phone service for days to attacks in a war in the next ten years.

location_factor.label: Your county is far from military sites, big cities, ports and refineries, so wartime attacks on infrastructure are less likely to reach it.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a house fire (about 3 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: Outages of power, water or phones for days, and shortages across the country.

register.name: Severe solar storm
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 7,600 and 1 in 150 households like yours would lose power for days to a severe solar storm in the next ten years.

location_factor.label: Your county is at a low geomagnetic latitude (about 38°). Solar storms drive the strongest currents into long power lines nearer the magnetic pole, so the chance of a long outage here is about 0.44 of the national average. The ground's conductivity also matters and is not counted.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than hail damage (about 8 in 1,000 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: Power out for days, and longer where large transformers fail.
register.what_it_changes: Nothing beyond your power plan: a solar storm harms long power lines, not phones or radios.

register.name: Power out for months (any cause)
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 2,900 and 1 in 62 households like yours would be without power for two months or more in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: A severe solar storm
sub_causes.note: Long outages where large transformers fail; most places would be back within days.

sub_causes.name: EMP from a nuclear attack
sub_causes.note: Only as part of a nuclear attack; EPRI's 2019 study did not support a nationwide blackout lasting months.

sub_causes.name: Attacks on the grid in a war
sub_causes.note: Cyberattacks, sabotage or missiles on power plants and lines.

sub_causes.name: Your county's own outage record
sub_causes.note: Storms and failures like the ones in your county's outage records, with the long tail the records cannot show yet.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a tornado (about 2 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: No power for months: water, heat, medicine and money all affected. Puerto Rico waited 328 days after Hurricane Maria.
register.what_it_changes: Nothing to stockpile for months. What helps instead: a way to treat water from a nearby source, a way to cook without power, a plan for toilets and waste, and some cash.

register.name: Nuclear attack or EMP
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 100,000 and 1 in 250 households like yours would be in a blast zone or under dangerous fallout in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Limited strike on US territory
sub_causes.note: One or a few weapons on US soil, for example a strike on Guam, Hawaii, Alaska or a West Coast base. It adds to your chance only where your county is a plausible target.

sub_causes.name: A crude nuclear device in a city
sub_causes.note: Heavy damage within about a mile, and everyone within 50 miles told to get inside. It adds to your chance by your metro area's share of FEMA's terrorism-preparedness money.

sub_causes.name: Electromagnetic pulse (EMP) from a high-altitude burst
sub_causes.note: Only as part of a nuclear attack: a burst high above the country could damage electronics and black out a region. EPRI's 2019 study found little damage to large transformers and did not support a nationwide blackout lasting months. The claim that most Americans would die rests on testimony that assumed such a blackout for a year, not on a published model.

sub_causes.name: Disruption across the country
sub_causes.note: Shortages, power cuts and lost income even far from any target. Shown for everyone and never added to your local chance.

sub_causes.name: A nuclear weapon used elsewhere in the world
sub_causes.note: At home: market shocks, shortages and worry, with no fallout of concern. Never added to your local chance.

location_factor.label: None of the places treated as likely targets, and no missile-field fallout path, is close to you. In a large nuclear war, the main effects here would be shortages, power cuts and lost income, not blast or heavy fallout.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than hail damage (about 8 in 1,000 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: Shortages, power cuts and lost income, not blast or heavy fallout.

register.name: Mass shooting or bombing
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 500,000 and 1 in 50,000 households like yours would have someone hurt in a mass shooting or bombing in the next ten years.

location_factor.label: The data are too sparse to say where this is more likely, so the chance is the same everywhere.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than an earthquake strong enough to knock things off shelves (about 1 in 1,000 for you in the next ten years).
register.what_it_changes: Nothing to buy. Two free steps: know "run, hide, fight", and learn to stop bleeding.

register.name: Chemical, biological or radiological attack
register.frequency_sentence: At most about 1 in 50,000 households like yours would be told to stay inside, or to collect medicine at a public site, after a chemical, biological or radiological attack in the next ten years, and perhaps fewer than 1 in 1,000,000.

sub_causes.name: Chemical
sub_causes.note: A toxic chemical released on purpose: shelter inside for hours, or leave the immediate area if told to.

sub_causes.name: Biological
sub_causes.note: A germ spread on purpose (the anthrax letters of 2001): stay home, and collect preventive medicine at a public site if told to.

sub_causes.name: Radiological ("dirty bomb")
sub_causes.note: Shelter inside for hours; the area may stay closed for weeks.

location_factor.label: Cameron Parish is outside the 44 urban areas FEMA funds for terrorism preparedness, so an attack that closes your area is much less likely than in the big cities.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than an earthquake strong enough to knock things off shelves (about 1 in 1,000 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: An order to stay inside for hours, closed buildings, or medicine handed out at public sites.
register.what_it_changes: Nothing beyond your basics: your three-day supplies cover sheltering inside.

buckets.name: No grid power at home
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 65 (60–85) will lose grid power for a day or more in the next 10 years.
Being ready for a week leaves about 9 (7–15) of 100 households like yours facing a longer power cut in the next 10 years.
This number mostly depends on how likely a direct hit by a major hurricane is (expert estimate) and how long power cuts from hurricanes and tropical storms last (from records).
Power cuts from storms here use your county's outage records since 2014, blended with about 150 nearby counties', because about eleven years is too short to see the rare storms.

The worst power cut in your region's records (where it was worst, about 55 miles (88 km) away) was Hurricane Laura (2020); being ready for a week would have left some homes that lost power still waiting (about 60 in 100 of all customers there were still out).

stress_test.region: your region's records (where it was worst, about 55 miles (88 km) away)

buckets.name: Tap water must be treated
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, fewer than 1 will have to boil or treat their tap water for a day or more in the next 10 years.
At the setting you chose (1 in 100 years), this is rare enough that there is no target.

buckets.name: No tap water at all
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 85 (80–95) will have no usable tap water for a day or more in the next 10 years.
Being ready for a month leaves about 6 (0–25) of 100 households like yours facing a longer water outage in the next 10 years.
This number mostly depends on how often droughts happen where you live (expert estimate) and how long water outages from drought lowering a well last (from records).
Your well pump runs on electricity, so every power cut is also a water cut. The pump itself also fails now and then (about once in 14 years).

buckets.name: Can't get to a store
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 60 (35–90) will be unable to shop for food and supplies for 3 days or more in the next 10 years.
Being ready for 2 weeks leaves about 7 (4–20) of 100 households like yours facing a longer stretch without shopping in the next 10 years.
This number mostly depends on how often pandemics happen where you live (expert estimate) and how long times without shopping from store shortages and runs on stores last (expert estimate).
This rounds up to 2 weeks: before rounding it is about 2 weeks, just past 10 days.

buckets.name: Dangerous heat or cold indoors
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 40 (35–60) will face dangerous heat or cold at home with no working cooling or heating for a day or more in the next 10 years.
Being ready for 5 days leaves about 8 (7–15) of 100 households like yours facing a longer spell of dangerous heat or cold in the next 10 years.
This number mostly depends on how likely a direct hit by a major hurricane is (expert estimate) and how often hurricanes and tropical storms happen where you live (expert estimate).
Your heating needs electricity to run (a gas furnace needs it for the igniter and fan), so a long winter power cut also cuts your heat.
A power cut during a heat wave also stops your air conditioning.

buckets.name: Medication and medical-supply continuity
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 80 (70–95) will have trouble getting medicine for 3 days or more in the next 10 years.
Being ready for 6 weeks leaves about 5 (3–20) of 100 households like yours facing a longer gap in medicine in the next 10 years.
This number mostly depends on how long gaps in medicine from a shortage of a daily prescription last (expert estimate) and how often medicine shortages happen where you live (expert estimate).
Medicine that must stay cold is at risk in any power cut longer than about a day, unless you have a cooler plan.
This rounds up to 6 weeks: before rounding it is about 4 weeks, just past a month.

buckets.name: No phone, internet or card payments
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 50 (30–90) will lose phone, internet or card payments for a day or more in the next 10 years.
Being ready for 5 days leaves about 5 (3–20) of 100 households like yours facing a longer outage in the next 10 years.

This number mostly depends on how long phone and payment outages from phone or internet network outages last (expert estimate) and how long phone and payment outages from short storm outages last (expert estimate).
This rounds up to 5 days: before rounding it is about 3.4 days, just past 3 days.

buckets.name: Must leave home quickly
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 95 (70–100) will have to leave home quickly at least once in the next 10 years.
Warning can be as short as a few minutes (a home fire) or as long as 3 days.
For chemical spills and releases, plan for as little as a few minutes of warning; for wildfires, 15 minutes.
Plan to be away for about 3 days.
Most evacuations last a few days, but after a home fire you could be away for 2 months or more.

buckets.name: Stranded away from home
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 80 (45–100) will have someone stranded away from home at least once in the next 10 years.
The 15-mile (24 km) trip is about 5 hours on foot; carry about 2 litres of water for it in hot weather.
The get-home bag is sized by the walk home at about 3 miles an hour, with about half a litre of water per hour in hot weather.

buckets.name: Medical emergency when help is slow
frequency_sentences: Households like yours average about 1 emergency-room visit a year (national figures).
Ambulances take longer to reach rural homes, so first-aid skills and supplies are worth more.

buckets.name: House fire
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 3 (2–3) will have a home fire at least once in the next 10 years.

buckets.name: Home and personal security
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 15 (9–25) will have a break-in or a nearby curfew at least once in the next 10 years.

buckets.name: Unhealthy air indoors
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 45 (25–75) will need to keep smoke, dust or fumes out of the home at least once in the next 10 years.
What helps: a room you can seal, an air cleaner or a box-fan filter, and well-fitting respirators for going outside.

buckets.name: Loss of income
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 25 (10–40) will have an income gap of more than 3 months in the next 10 years.
Aim for about 7 months of income in savings over time, a goal separate from the supplies budget.
This number mostly depends on how long income gaps from losing a job last (expert estimate) and how often job losses happen where you live (expert estimate).
The death or long-term disability of an earner is a question for life and disability insurance, not savings.

buckets.name: Home damaged or uninhabitable
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 30 (20–45) will have to leave home for a while because of damage at least once in the next 10 years.
After a disaster, most displaced households are back within a month, but about 1 in 10 homeowners never return, so insurance and copies of documents matter more than supplies here.

If damage forced you out, 9 in 10 households like yours would be home again within about 13 months; living elsewhere that long costs about $14,000 at 30% of your monthly spending, which loss-of-use insurance pays for.

scenarios.name: Direct hit by a major hurricane
scenarios.applies_because: Tropical storms and hurricanes reach Cameron Parish about once every 6 years, and about 1 in 9 of them is a major storm (Category 3 or stronger) that can cut power and water for weeks. Hurricane guidance in Louisiana covers it, so the plan includes it.
scenarios.effect_summary: Planning for it changes: Power: 5 days → 7 days; Food and supplies: 10 days → 14 days; Medicine: 30 days → 45 days; Phone and payments: 3 days → 5 days; households like yours that have to leave home quickly within 10 years: 93 → 94 in 100.

items.name: Set up emergency alerts and know how to reach 911

requirements.plain: 2 battery lights: a headlamp or lantern for each person aged 4 and over. Use lights, not candles. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
1 pack of AA or AAA batteries for the lights and the radio: one pack lasts a household about 7 days. Check which sizes your lights use. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)

1 pair of appliance thermometers, one in the fridge and one in the freezer: after a power cut, keep refrigerated food only if it stayed at 40 °F or below, and throw out perishable food that was above 40 °F for 2 hours or more. (Ready.gov)

1 battery power station (about 1,070 Wh each) to keep refrigerated medicine cool through a 7-day power cut, because a cooler bag lasts only about 1 day. Your essential load (phones) is about 30 Wh a day, 210 Wh for 7 days; one station gives about 910 Wh after losses, enough for about 30.3 days of that load. A full-size fridge alone would drain one in about 0.9 days. It can run a small 12-volt cooler for the medicine, or the fridge in short spells. Recharge it from a car, gas or electric, with the engine running outdoors only, or from a solar panel. (retail prices, ENERGY STAR, CDC; some amounts are estimates)

Optional: a portable generator can run the fridge and lights through a 7-day outage. It must run outdoors, at least 20 feet from windows, doors and vents, never in a garage, and it needs fuel (see the fuel line). To run the well pump it must supply the pump's starting watts, 2 to 3 times its running watts, and 240 volts if the pump runs on 240 (check the nameplate), and it reaches the pump only through an inlet with an interlock or transfer switch that an electrician installs. Never plug a generator into a wall outlet: backfeeding can electrocute utility workers. (CDC, Ready.gov, Ready Reckoner research, CPSC; some amounts are estimates)

Optional for a 7-day outage: a portable solar panel with a battery. In December a 100 W panel near your latitude makes about 382 Wh a day (like Miami, FL (Phoenix, AZ makes 424)). Your essential load of about 30 Wh a day needs about 10 W of panels in full sun; a full-size fridge would need about 260 W. Panels laid flat or in shade make less. (NREL PVWatts, ENERGY STAR; some amounts are estimates)

Optional: keeping a fridge running takes about 995 Wh a day (a chest freezer about 597) × 7 days = 6,970 Wh. A closed fridge keeps food cold about 4 hours and a full freezer about 48; shelf-stable food avoids the need. (ENERGY STAR, Ready.gov)

Optional: your well pump needs about 1,250 W to run (1,000 to 1,500) and 2 to 3 times that to start; check its nameplate. At 1 hour a day that is 8,750 Wh for 7 days. A battery power station usually cannot start it; a generator or a hand pump can. Stored water is the cheaper way to cover this. (an estimate)

2 people × 1 gallon a day × 14 days = 28 gallons, plus 4.4 gallons for the dog: about 32.4 gallons. Replace water you store yourself every 6 months. Your target is 30 days. Storing all of it would take about 69.4 gallons, so the plan stores the first 14 days and makes the rest safe with a filter and a water source (see the next line). (Ready.gov, CDC, PetMD, BYU; some amounts are estimates)

Free first step: fill clean drink bottles you already have with tap water, about 6 gallons, the most a household can usually gather this way. Not milk jugs: they leak. Label them and replace the water every 6 months. (Ready Reckoner research, CDC, Ready.gov, Church of Jesus Christ; some amounts are estimates)

After day 14, for the other 16 days: make about 2.3 gallons of water safe each day, about 37 gallons in all, with a water filter and water from your well, which needs a way to run its pump in a power cut (a generator connected through an interlock or transfer switch an electrician installs, or a hand pump), instead of storing more. Filter it, then boil it for 1 minute (3 minutes above 5,000 feet), or add 8 drops of 6 % unscented bleach per gallon (6 drops of 8.25 %) and wait 30 minutes; double the bleach for cloudy or very cold water. No agency sets a one-month amount: this step sits between the two-week advice (Red Cross, Oregon, Washington) and the Church's three-month pantry. (Ready.gov, CDC, PetMD, BYU; some amounts are estimates)

2 water carriers of about 5 gallons each for hauling water from a distribution point, a neighbour's well or a spring, because your target of 30 days runs past the 14 days of water you store, and the rest has to come from somewhere. A full one weighs about 42 pounds, so choose a size you can carry, with a good handle. (retail prices, EPA; some amounts are estimates)

1 bottle of plain unscented bleach (5 to 9 % sodium hypochlorite, not the splashless kind), for making water safe and for cleaning, however long your target is. At about 0.5 mL a gallon, each ounce treats about 60 gallons of clear water (30 if it is cloudy or very cold), so one bottle treats thousands of gallons. Bleach weakens in storage: buy a fresh bottle every 6 months, when you replace the water you store yourself. (CDC, EPA; some amounts are estimates)

4 large animals × 25 L a day (20 to 30) × 14 days = 1,400 L, about 369.8 gallons. Fill tubs or stock tanks before a storm or an outage. Your target is 30 days; store the first 14 days, as for people, instead of buying more tank space. A power cut longer than that needs a generator that can start the well pump, connected through an interlock or transfer switch an electrician installs; in a drought that lowers the well, haul water in, and a stock tank holds what you haul. (Sphere, ASPCA, BYU, Church of Jesus Christ; some amounts are estimates)

1 food-grade tote of about 275 gallons that fits a pickup, to haul water when a drought dries the well: the 4 large animals drink about 26.4 gallons a day, so one load lasts about 10.4 days. (retail prices, Sphere, ASPCA)
A two-bucket toilet for when toilets can't flush: 2 sturdy buckets with a seat, one for pee and one for poo. (RDPO, Oregon OEM)

Toilet bags: about 0.45 heavy garbage bags a person a day (0.3 to 0.6), counting both bags of a double-bagged load: 2 people × 30 days = 27 bags. Fill halfway, tie, double-bag, and store away from food, water, children and pets. Don't put them in curbside trash or bury them unless officials say so. (RDPO, Oregon OEM; some amounts are estimates)

Cover material for the poo bucket (sawdust, shredded paper, dry leaves or pet bedding): about 1 cup a person a day (0.5 to 1.5) × 2 people × 30 days = 60 cups, about 3.8 gallons. (RDPO; some amounts are estimates)

3 household kits of paper plates, cups and utensils, garbage bags with ties, and waterproof matches, one for every 14 days of your 30-day no-water target: paper plates save the water that washing dishes takes. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)

1 adult at about 2,262 kcal a day and 1 person 65 or over at about 2,009 kcal a day: about 4,271 kcal a day × 14 days = 59,800 kcal. These are moderately active needs; the form does not ask sex, so men's and women's needs are averaged. Count calories, not servings. (Dietary Guidelines)

As everyday groceries: about $260 for 28 person-days (USDA Thrifty Food Plan, $8.44 a person a day, plus 10 % for a household of 2). Buy what you already eat, keep it in the pantry and use the oldest first. (USDA)

As bulk staples such as wheat, rice and beans: about $70 ($2.15 to $2.85 a person a day). Cheapest, but it needs cooking and is short on some vitamins, so it suits months rather than days. (Church of Jesus Christ, BYU)

As freeze-dried or dehydrated meals: about $717 ($9 to $39 per 2,000 kcal, so $269 to $1,166). They need about 0.6 gallons of extra water a person a day to prepare. (Dietary Guidelines, retail prices; some amounts are estimates)

A retail "30-day" food kit supplies about 1,290 to 1,730 kcal a day. For the average person here (about 2,135 kcal a day) one lasts about 18 to 24 days, not 30. Compare kits by total kcal. (Dietary Guidelines, retail prices)

Dry food for the dog for 14 days (at least a week): about 0.7 lb a day for each dog = 9.8 lb. Feed what the label says for yours, and keep it in an airtight, waterproof container. (ASPCA, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
Food for the dog for 14 days (14 pet-days, at least a week): what it eats now, in an airtight, waterproof container. (ASPCA, Ready.gov)

A way to cook and boil water without power, because your plan runs 14 days without a store, longer than food that needs no cooking comfortably covers: a camp stove, one that burns propane, because winter outages come where you live: butane stops turning to gas near 32 °F, propane not until about -44 °F. Use it outdoors only, never indoors or in a garage (carbon monoxide), and keep a lighter or waterproof matches with it. (Oregon OEM, CDC, NIST; some amounts are estimates)

Fuel for a propane camp stove: about 0.2 lb of fuel a person a day × 2 people × 14 days = 5.6 lb, or 6 one-pound propane cylinders. Use the stove outdoors only (carbon monoxide), and store the cylinders outside the living space, with no more than 2 inside the home or an attached garage. (CDC, Ready Reckoner research, EIA, retail prices; some amounts are estimates)

Optional, if you have an outdoor gas grill: a spare filled 20-pound cylinder is the cheapest way to boil water and cook in a long outage. Use the grill outdoors only, away from the house, and keep the cylinder outside, never indoors or in the garage. (local fire code, CDC)
Toilet paper: about 1 roll a person every 5 days × 2 people × 14 days = 6 rolls. Better still, measure a week's use and double it for two weeks. (Oregon OEM; some amounts are estimates)
Soap for 2 person-months: 2 people × 1 month. Each is 250 g of bathing soap and 200 g of laundry soap, about 900 g in all. (Sphere)

Period products for 2 cycles each, about 20 products a cycle (15 to 30). The form doesn't ask sex, so the plan counts half of the 1 person aged 13 to 64 who are not pregnant or nursing: 1 cycle's worth, about 20 products. Keep soap, clean underwear and pain relievers with them, and put used products in a separate bag. (CDC, Sphere, Oregon OEM; some amounts are estimates)
2 warm blankets, one for each person: most homes already have them. (Ready.gov, Sphere)
2 sets of warm layers (coat, hat, gloves, dry socks), one for each person. (Ready.gov, CDC)

2 sleeping bags or extra heavy blankets, one for each person, rated for the coldest nights where you live: your cold target of 5 days is longer than the 3 days that blankets and warm layers cover. (Ready.gov, Sphere; some amounts are estimates)

A cold plan: pick one room to keep warm, close off the others, put towels under doors and cover windows at night, and find your nearest warming centre in case the home gets too cold. Never heat with a gas oven, grill, camp stove or generator indoors (carbon monoxide). Gas, oil and propane furnaces usually need electricity for their fans and controls, so plan for cold without power. People 65 and over should check the indoor temperature often. A body temperature below 95 °F needs medical help at once. (CDC, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)

2 people take prescription medicine every day: keep 30 days of it on hand each (60 person-days). Your target is 45 days; beyond 30 days, ask your prescriber or insurer about a longer fill. Keep a written list of each medicine, what it is for and the dose. After a disaster declaration some states let pharmacies give an emergency refill of up to 30 days, and many allow only a few days; ask your pharmacist what yours allows. For medicine the plan keeps at most a month on hand: agencies advise 7 days to two weeks (Red Cross, CDC, Florida), and a longer target is kept up with 60- to 90-day fills from your drug plan (Medicare). (Florida DEM, CDC, Red Cross, Healthcare Ready)

Your medication target is 45 days; the reserve at home covers the first 30 days. For the other 15 days, ask your drug plan whether it offers 60 to 90 day fills and which pharmacies give them, and refill as soon as the plan allows, so the supply at home stays ahead of each refill (30 person-days in all). (Florida DEM, CDC, Red Cross, Medicare)

1 person needs medicine kept cold, such as insulin. An insulated bag with fresh cold packs keeps it cool, never frozen, for about 1 day. Insulin in its vial or pen keeps working up to 28 days between 59 °F and 86 °F, so in a longer power cut keep it in the shade and below 86 °F; never use insulin that froze. Your power target is 7 days: plan a battery power station to run a small 12-volt cooler or the fridge (see its line), and a place with power you could go to. (FDA, CDC; some amounts are estimates)

No antibiotics are included in this plan. If you have a specific, foreseeable need, such as remote travel, talk to your own clinician about a standby prescription with written instructions. Never use fish or pet antibiotics, never share prescriptions, and don't use expired ones. (CDC, FDA)
1 battery or hand-crank radio that gets NOAA Weather Radio, with a tone alert, for warnings when phones and power are down. (Ready.gov, NOAA)
Power banks: 2 phones × about 15 Wh a day (10 to 20) × 7 days without power = 210 Wh. Text instead of calling to save battery. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)

2 two-way radios for the 2 people aged 13 and over, to reach each other when phones are down. FRS radios need no licence; GMRS radios reach farther but need a $35 FCC licence that covers the family for 10 years. (FCC; some amounts are estimates)
2 written contact cards, one for each person aged 4 and over: an out-of-area contact, meeting places and key numbers. Phones die; paper does not. (Ready.gov)
1 paper map of your area, marked with meeting places and ways out. Save offline maps on your phone too. (Ready.gov)

Cash in small bills, kept with your documents, because ATMs and cards may not work in an outage: about $180: half of 3 days of your usual spending ($3,600 a month), the part that goes on food, fuel and medicine. No agency gives a dollar amount. (Ready.gov, FEMA; some amounts are estimates)

2 go-bags, one for each person: a sturdy bag you already own will do. Pack copies of documents on paper and on a flash drive, a phone charger, cash, a flashlight, a whistle, an old pair of prescription glasses, a change of clothes and sturdy shoes, and add water, food and medicines from your home supplies rather than buying them twice. You may get only minutes of warning (a local tsunami or a fast fire), so keep the bags packed by the door, and one at work if you work in a danger zone. Practise grabbing them and leaving. Plan where you would stay for about 3 days. (Washington EMD, Ready.gov, CDC; some amounts are estimates)

Water for the go-bags comes out of the water you store at home, not on top of it: the Red Cross three-day supply for leaving home, about 2 gallons a day for the 2 people × 3 days = 6 gallons. Keep it with the bags or take it as you leave. If you leave on foot, carry what you can (about 2.5 L each) and a filter; the rest goes in the car. (Red Cross, Washington EMD, Ready.gov, CDC; some amounts are estimates)

Food for the go-bags comes out of your home food supply, not on top of it: about 4,271 kcal a day × 3 days = 12,800 kcal of food that needs no cooking or refrigeration. (Red Cross, Washington EMD, Dietary Guidelines)

1 pet carrier, one for each pet, with a pet go-kit: water and food from your home supplies, any medicine it takes, records and a photo. Public shelters may take only service animals, so find pet-friendly places to stay ahead of time. (ASPCA, Ready.gov)
Water for the pet go-kit, set aside from your stored water rather than bought extra: 7 days for the dog = 2.2 gallons. Replace it every 2 months. (ASPCA, PetMD; some amounts are estimates)
Food for the pet go-kit, set aside from your pet food rather than bought extra: 10 days (7 to 10 days) for the dog = 10 pet-days. Replace it every 2 months. (ASPCA)
Keep the vehicle at least half full at all times, and fill up when leaving looks likely. (Ready.gov)

Person 1 travels 14.9 miles (24 km) by car to work or school; walking home at about 3 mph takes about 5 hours. Keep a get-home bag in the car: comfortable walking shoes, a light, a paper map, cash in small bills, a rain or warm layer, and water and snacks from home. Be ready to stay at work for 24 hours if you can't leave. (FHWA, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
Water for person 1's walk home: 5 hours × about 0.5 L an hour = 2.5 L, in a bottle filled from home rather than bought extra. (FHWA; some amounts are estimates)

Snacks for person 1's walk home: about 500 kcal for 5 hours on foot (about 1,250 kcal every 12 hours), from your food at home rather than bought extra. (FHWA, Dietary Guidelines; some amounts are estimates)

1 car emergency kit: jumper cables or a charged jump pack you have tried, a flashlight, warm clothes, a blanket, bottled water and snacks, and your roadside-assistance number on paper; sand or cat litter in snow country. (Ready.gov)

1 family first-aid kit for 2 people: the Red Cross list for a family of 4 (bandages, gauze, tape, antiseptic wipes, gloves, a breathing barrier, a cold pack, tweezers, an emergency blanket and a thermometer). Add your own medicines and emergency numbers, and replace what you use. (Red Cross)

1 package of each of 4 kinds of non-prescription medicine (a pain reliever, an anti-diarrhea medicine, an antacid and an allergy medicine): one package of each lasts about 14 days for 4 people. That is 4 packages for 14 days. Follow the label, and ask a pharmacist about children's versions. (Ready.gov, CDC, Red Cross; some amounts are estimates)
1 oral thermometer (non-mercury, non-glass; it is on the Red Cross kit list). (Red Cross)

Oral rehydration salts for vomiting, diarrhea or heat illness: 3 packets a person for every 2 weeks, at least 2 weeks' worth. For 2 people and 14 days that is 6 packets. Mix each packet into 1 litre of safe water. (CDC; some amounts are estimates)

1 bleeding-control kit: a tourniquet and a pressure bandage for serious bleeding, and a Stop the Bleed class so you know how to use them. Serious bleeding can kill before help arrives. Ambulances take longer to reach rural homes, so keep it where everyone can find it fast. (DHS, JAMA Surgery)

A wound-care and splint add-on for the first-aid kit: an irrigation syringe to wash a wound with clean water, wound-closure strips, an elastic wrap, a padded splint, trauma shears, blister dressings and gauze for packing a deep wound. Washing a wound out with plenty of clean water is the key step. Ambulances take longer to reach rural homes, so keep it with the first-aid kit. (Wilderness Medical Society, Red Cross, JAMA Surgery)

A fire escape plan: two ways out of every room, a meeting spot outside, and a practice run with everyone. Upstairs bedrooms need a second way out, such as a window onto a porch roof or an escape ladder (see the ladder line). (Ready.gov)

No smoke alarms yet: one on every level and in every bedroom, about 2 levels and 1 bedroom for a home like yours = 3 alarms. Ask your fire department or the Red Cross first: some fire departments and the Red Cross install free smoke alarms. Buy them only if they cannot. Test them every month. (USFA, Ready.gov, Red Cross; some amounts are estimates)

No fire extinguisher yet: 2 multipurpose (A-B-C) extinguishers, one on each of the 2 floors a home like yours has, the ground-floor one near the kitchen. If your kitchen is on another floor, keep one there too. Learn how to use one before you need it. Small home fires are common: CPSC estimated about 6.6 a year for every 100 households, most of them cooking fires, and fire departments attend only about 3 in 100 of them. (USFA, CPSC; some amounts are estimates)

A house like yours usually has bedrooms upstairs (2 levels): 1 two-storey escape ladder for an upstairs bedroom window, in case fire or smoke blocks the stairs. Skip it if every bedroom is on the ground floor or already has a second way out, such as a porch roof. Keep it by the window and practise with it. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
Swap phone numbers with 2 neighbours and agree who checks on whom after a storm or an outage, when phones and roads may be down. (an estimate)

N95 respirators, for about 5 days of smoke, dust or ash: 1 a day for each of the 2 people aged 13 and over = 10 respirators. A well-fitting N95 protects far more than a cloth or surgical mask; replace it when breathing through it gets harder. (CDC; some amounts are estimates)

1 portable air cleaner with a HEPA filter for your clean room: for a room of about 200 square feet, a clean air delivery rate (CADR) of at least 130 for smoke (EPA's sizing, more for high ceilings). Keep a spare filter, and avoid air cleaners that make ozone. (EPA; some amounts are estimates)

Cheaper than an air cleaner: a 20-inch box fan with a 20 by 20 inch MERV 13 filter taped to its intake side, which EPA calls a cost-effective way to cut smoke indoors. Use a newer fan with safety features, and do not leave it running while no one is home. (EPA)

A clean-room plan for smoky or dusty days: pick one room with few windows and doors where everyone can sleep, keep it closed, set the heating or cooling to recirculate (or turn off fans that pull in outside air), run the air cleaner there, and do not fry food, burn candles or vacuum on those days. (EPA, CDC)

Savings goal: about 7 months of expenses ($25,200 at $3,600 a month), built up over time and kept apart from the supplies budget. You have about 2 months saved now. Planners often suggest 3 to 6 months; the CFPB says it depends on your situation. (FINRA, St. Louis Fed, CFPB)

Someone in your household earns money the others rely on: check whether your job offers disability insurance, and whether life insurance would carry the others through the years they would need. About 1 in 4 workers who start at 20 become disabled before retirement age. NAIC's buyer's guide helps you work out how much cover is enough. (SSA, NAIC)

Copy the 4 parts of FEMA's Emergency Financial First Aid Kit: IDs, financial and legal papers (including insurance), medical information, and household contacts. Keep copies in a waterproof, fire-resistant place or with someone you trust, with photos of your home and belongings, and update them once a year. (FEMA)

Home and renters policies usually don't cover floods. Decide on flood insurance before you need it: about 3 in 10 flood insurance claims come from outside high-risk flood areas. A quote costs nothing, and a new policy usually starts 30 days after you buy it. It pays up to $250,000 for the building and $100,000 for belongings. (FEMA, FloodSmart, Ready.gov)

Hurricanes drive your home-loss risk: check your policy for a separate hurricane or windstorm deductible. In some places it is a percentage of the home's insured value rather than a dollar amount, and coastal policies can leave out wind damage altogether. Find the amount on the declarations page and add it to your savings goal. (NAIC)

warnings.message: You own your home in a flood-prone area and have no flood insurance.
warnings.why: Standard home policies do not cover flooding, and a new flood policy usually has a waiting period before it starts. Get a quote before storm season.

para.t:
**For:** 1 adult and 1 older adult, with 1 dog and 4 large animals  
**Where:** Cameron Parish, Louisiana (ZIP code 70631)  
**Home:** an owned house on rural land, with a private well, propane heat and window air conditioning  
**Plan date:** October 1, 2026  
**Ready for:** very serious disruptions (the 1-in-100 setting), in today's climate. Water is planned at the basic level, about 1 gallon a person a day.[1]
> Ready Reckoner is an independent, open-source planning aid. It is not official emergency guidance, and not medical, legal or financial advice. Follow instructions from your local officials first.

**Where you are now:** getting started. **What is enough for your risks:** three months of supplies. At your budget, the bare minimum (three days of water, light, warmth and medicine) is in place by month 4 (February 2027), and everything by month 25 (November 2028). Start with the free steps under Your plan.
### The three things that matter most

1. Of 100 households like yours, about 95 (70–100) will have to leave home quickly at least once in the next 10 years. Parts of your area flood in a hurricane's storm surge.[2] Know your evacuation zone and where you would go; leave when told.[3, 4] For chemical spills and releases, plan for as little as a few minutes of warning; for wildfires, 15 minutes.[5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11]
2. Of 100 households like yours, about 65 (60–85) will lose grid power for a day or more in the next 10 years. If you are not told to leave, be ready to manage about 7 days at home with no power, and about 1 month with no tap water.
3. Of 100 households like yours, about 60 (35–90) will be unable to shop for food and supplies for 3 days or more in the next 10 years. Keep about 2 weeks of food you normally eat, and 1½ months of daily medicine on hand.

**What the plan assumes you already have:** a charged mobile phone, go-bag for each person, manual can opener, a cooking pot with a lid, three days of the food you normally eat, a warm blanket for each person and warm layers for each person. If any is missing, untick "Assume everyday basics" on the Have screen and the plan will add it.
Fill this in together, here or on the "Your family plan" screen. Keep a copy in each go-bag and one on the fridge: phones die.[12]

### Leaving home

Warning can be as short as a few minutes (a home fire) or as long as 3 days. For chemical spills and releases, plan for as little as a few minutes of warning; for wildfires, 15 minutes. Plan to be away for about 3 days. Most evacuations last a few days, but after a home fire you could be away for 2 months or more.[5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11]
### Staying in touch

**Four ways to reach each other.** Emergency planners call this a PACE plan: a primary way, an alternate, a contingency and an emergency way. Each one takes over when the one before it fails.[13] For a household it can be:

1. Primary: call.
2. Alternate: text. A text may get through when a call does not, and it saves battery.[14]
3. Contingency: everyone texts one out-of-state contact, who passes the news along.[14]
4. Emergency: go to the place you agreed to meet if you get separated.[14]
Cut out a card for each person's wallet or phone case.

### Medicine

- 2 people take prescription medicine every day: keep 30 days of it on hand each (60 person-days). Your target is 45 days; beyond 30 days, ask your prescriber or insurer about a longer fill. Keep a written list of each medicine, what it is for and the dose. After a disaster declaration some states let pharmacies give an emergency refill of up to 30 days, and many allow only a few days; ask your pharmacist what yours allows. For medicine the plan keeps at most a month on hand: agencies advise 7 days to two weeks (Red Cross, CDC, Florida), and a longer target is kept up with 60- to 90-day fills from your drug plan (Medicare).[6, 7, 9, 11, 41, 49, 50, 57, 58, 116, 147, 167, 177, 178, 179, 180]
- 1 person needs medicine kept cold, such as insulin. An insulated bag with fresh cold packs keeps it cool, never frozen, for about 1 day. Insulin in its vial or pen keeps working up to 28 days between 59 °F and 86 °F, so in a longer power cut keep it in the shade and below 86 °F; never use insulin that froze. Your power target is 7 days: plan a battery power station to run a small 12-volt cooler or the fridge (see its line), and a place with power you could go to. ### Antibiotics

### What to know and do
#### 1. Medical emergency
Nearly every household like yours will have someone need emergency care in the next ten years.[15, 16]
**Includes:** far from emergency care; falls.

**What helps.** Take a first-aid and bleeding-control class. You may be able to save a life by acting right after an injury, before help arrives.[17] If a teen or adult collapses and their heart stops, call 911 and push hard and fast in the center of the chest. This hands-only CPR needs no training. Note where the nearest heart defibrillator (AED) is; it talks you through each step.[18] Keep a stocked first-aid kit. Check it regularly and replace anything used or out of date.[19] Keep a list of each person's medicines, doses and allergies with your emergency supplies.[20] Know how to reach 911. Call if you can, and text where that service works.[21]
**What to avoid.** Do not start antibiotics on your own or take someone else's. The wrong medicine can delay the right treatment and cause serious side effects.[22] Do not use expired medicines.[23]
**How bad:** Serious (based on data).
#### 2. Wildfire
Of 100 households like yours, about 88 (38 to nearly all) will have to leave home or lose power because of a wildfire in the next ten years.[6, 11]

**What helps.** Keep a zone at least 30 feet around your home clear of leaves, debris and anything that burns.[24] Know your evacuation zone and routes, and practice with your pets.[24] Store N95 masks for smoke. Pick a room you can close off from outside air, and run a portable air cleaner there.[24] N95 masks are not made to fit children, so for them the clean room is the protection.[25] A box fan with a MERV 13 filter makes a low-cost air cleaner.[26] If your heating and cooling system brings in fresh air, set it to recirculate.[24] Keep phones charged and have backup chargers.[24]

**What to avoid.** Leave as soon as authorities tell you to, even if you cannot see flames.[24] Do not use an air cleaner that makes ozone.[27] Avoid hard exercise when it is smoky, so you breathe in less smoke.[27]
**How bad:** Serious (rough data).
#### 3. Hurricane
Of 100 households like yours, about 78 (62–91) will lose power or have damage from a hurricane or tropical storm in the next ten years.[6, 7, 8, 10, 11]
**Includes:** inland flooding from a tropical storm.

**What helps.** Know your evacuation zone, your routes and where you would stay. If you live in a mandatory evacuation zone and officials tell you to leave, go right away.[4] If you are not told to leave, shelter from the wind in a small inside room, closet or hallway away from windows, on the lowest floor that will not flood.[4, 28] Clear drains and gutters, bring in outdoor furniture, and think about storm shutters. Keep phones charged and have backup chargers.[4] A flood policy typically takes up to 30 days to start, so buy it well before a storm.[29] If you would leave in an electric car, keep it fully charged all hurricane season.[30]

**What to avoid.** Never walk or drive through floodwater. One foot of moving water can sweep a car away.[29] Do not drive or charge an electric car that has been in floodwater. Salt water can start a battery fire.[30] Never run a generator inside your home or garage.[31]
**How bad:** Serious (mostly data).
#### 4. Lightning
Of 100 households like yours, about 15 (4–43) will have lightning damage their home or cut their power in the next ten years.[6, 11]

**What helps.** Pick your shelter spot now. A safe room or storm shelter is best.[32] The next best is a small, windowless room or basement on the lowest floor of a sturdy building.[32, 33] Sign up for your community's warnings, and learn what your sirens sound like.[32] Know the signs of a tornado: a rotating funnel cloud, a cloud of debris, or a roar like a freight train. In your shelter, protect your head and neck with your arms, and pile blankets or cushions around you.[32] When thunder roars, go indoors. Get into a building or a car with a roof.[34]

**What to avoid.** Stay away from windows, doors and outside walls.[32] There is no safe place in a car during a tornado, only less dangerous ones. If you are caught, stay buckled in and keep your head below the windows.[32] During a thunderstorm, avoid running water and electronics plugged into the wall.[34]
**How bad:** Very severe (rough data).
#### 5. Burst pipe or water leak
Of 100 households like yours, about 14 will have a burst pipe or leak flood part of the home in the next ten years.[35]
**Includes:** sewer backup.

**What helps.** Find your main water shut-off valve now, and show everyone how to turn it off. A burst pipe can flood a room quickly.[36, 37] Once a year, check the hoses to the water heater, washing machine, dishwasher and fridge, and replace any that crack or leak. A leak alarm can warn you early.[36] In freezing weather, let a faucet drip at night, open the cabinet doors under sinks on outside walls, and keep the heat at 55°F or higher.[37] Home and renters policies usually cover burst pipes. Many do not cover a sewer backup unless you add that cover, and floods need their own policy.[36]

**What to avoid.** Never thaw a frozen pipe with an open flame; use a hair dryer. Watch for electric shock around standing water.[37] Do not leave home while the washing machine or dishwasher is running.[36]
**How bad:** Severe (mostly data).
#### 6. Coastal flooding
Of 100 households like yours, about 9 will have coastal flooding reach their home in the next ten years.[5, 6]

**What helps.** Look up your address on FEMA's flood maps, and sign up for your community's warnings.[29] Homeowner's insurance does not cover flooding, and a flood policy typically takes up to 30 days to start.[29] Renters can buy flood coverage for their belongings.[38] Know how you would get to higher ground or a higher floor.[29]

**What to avoid.** Six inches of moving water can knock you down, and one foot can sweep your car away.[29] Never drive around barriers on a flooded road. The road may have collapsed under the water.[39] Stay off bridges over fast-moving water.[29] Leave if you are told to.[40]
**How bad:** Very severe (mostly data).
#### 7. House fire
Of 100 households like yours, about 3 will have a house fire in the next ten years.[41]
**Includes:** carbon monoxide poisoning; lithium battery fire.

**What helps.** Put smoke alarms inside and outside every bedroom and on every level, and test them each month.[42] Practice your escape plan twice a year, including finding your way out in the dark.[43] Sleep with bedroom doors closed. Teach children not to hide from firefighters.[43] If there is smoke, crawl low under it to your exit.[43] If you cannot get out, close the door, cover vents and cracks with cloth or tape, call 911, and signal from the window with a light-colored cloth or a flashlight.[43] Insurance and copies of your documents help you recover afterward.[44]

**What to avoid.** Before you open a door, feel the door and the knob. If either is hot, or smoke is coming around it, keep it closed and use your second way out.[43] If a person or pet is still inside, get out and tell firefighters right away.[43] If your clothes catch fire, stop, drop and roll.[43]
**How bad:** Severe (based on data).
#### 8. Tornado
Of 100 households like yours, about 2 (1–6) will have a tornado damage or cut off their neighborhood in the next ten years.[6, 11]
**What helps.** The steps under "Lightning" above apply here too.
**How bad:** Very severe (rough data).

### Safety rules to learn now

- **Food:** In a power cut, throw out food that has been at 40°F or warmer for 2 hours.[91]

pages.title: When a storm, freeze or heat wave is forecast

para.t: Hurricanes, winter storms and heat waves usually come with warning. Keep your phone charged when one is forecast, and use the time the same way each time.[4]
**Before any storm**

- Charge phones, power banks and other batteries.[136] 
- Fill the car's tank and get some cash, since card readers and cash machines need power.[136] Charge the power station.[136] If you would leave in an electric car, charge it fully.[30]
- Refill prescriptions if you can.[136]
- Fill the bathtub and other large containers with water for flushing and cleaning.[136]
- Turn the fridge to its coldest setting and keep the doors shut.[136] A full freezer keeps food cold for about 48 hours, a fridge for about four.[91]
- Bring in or tie down outdoor furniture and grills.[4]
- Check your evacuation zone and your plan to leave.[4]
- Check with neighbors, older adults and anyone who may need help.[4]

**Before a hard freeze.** Let hot and cold water drip from a faucet at night, open the cabinet doors under sinks on outside walls, and keep the heat at 55°F or higher. Make sure everyone knows how to shut off the water in case a pipe bursts.[37]

**Before a heat wave.** Pick a place to cool down, such as a library, or ask your local health department about cooling options. Plan to check on family, older adults and neighbors. Fans do not lower body temperature.[110]

pages.title: After a disaster: the first 30 days

para.t: **Your county.** Cameron Parish, Louisiana had 3 federal major-disaster declarations in the last five full years.[159]
Recovery takes weeks. These steps come in rough order.

**Going home.** Go back only when local officials say it is safe. Do not go inside if you smell gas or the building looks damaged.[160] Run a generator only outside, more than 20 feet from windows, doors and vents.[31]

**Insurance and records.** Before you clean up, take photos and videos and make a list of the damage.[160] Keep every receipt.[161] Call your insurer as soon as you can, and an adjuster will come to inspect. Check the adjuster's estimate, and talk to them before you sign a repair contract.[162]
**Help from FEMA.** If a federal disaster declaration covers your county, apply at DisasterAssistance.gov or call 1-800-621-3362.[163] FEMA help does not replace insurance.[164]

**Scams.** FEMA never charges to apply or to inspect.[165] Its inspectors carry an official photo ID and never ask for your bank details; a FEMA shirt is not an ID.[161] Never sign your insurance check over to a contractor, and walk away from anyone who wants cash up front.[166]

**Medicine.** In a declared disaster, Medicare drug plans can help you find a pharmacy and replace lost medicine.[167] Many states let a pharmacist give an emergency supply when your prescriber cannot be reached, and the rules differ by state.[147] Healthcare Ready's Rx Open map shows which pharmacies are open in a disaster area.[168]
**Papers.** To replace lost IDs, start with your birth certificate, from the vital records office of the state where you were born.[169]

**How likely here.** From your own power curve, power out for two months or more: between 1 in 3,000 and 1 in 660 households like yours in the next 10 years; for three months or more: between 1 in 13,000 and 1 in 2,400.[5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 95, 96]
These pointers are for the rare event that lasts for months. They are places to start, not a manual.

**Rain.** Each state sets its own rules on collecting rain, and the rules vary widely, so check yours.[170] Rainwater is not safe to drink until germs and chemicals are removed, but it can water plants you do not eat.[171]

**Wells.** A well pump stops when the power goes out. Have a licensed electrician connect any generator.[172] A hand pump fitted to the well can still draw water in a long outage; test and treat that water before drinking it.[173]
**Toilets.** After a strong earthquake, toilets may not flush for weeks or months. A twin-bucket toilet keeps pee and poo apart, and handling poo safely stops diseases like cholera.[102]

**Food.** Badly home-canned food can cause botulism. Vegetables, meat and fish need a pressure canner.[174] Use tested recipes, such as those from the National Center for Home Food Preservation.[175] Your state or county Extension service can help with growing and preserving food.[174]
**Spirits.** Keep regular sleep and wake times, take breaks from the news, and talk with people you trust.[176] Keep books, games and puzzles for children.[140]

# Your preparedness packet

**For:** 1 adult and 1 older adult, with 1 dog and 4 large animals  
**Where:** Cameron Parish, Louisiana (ZIP code 70631)  
**Home:** an owned house on rural land, with a private well, propane heat and window air conditioning  
**Plan date:** October 1, 2026  
**Ready for:** very serious disruptions (the 1-in-100 setting), in today's climate. Water is planned at the basic level, about 1 gallon a person a day.[1]

> Ready Reckoner is an independent, open-source planning aid. It is not official emergency guidance, and not medical, legal or financial advice. Follow instructions from your local officials first.

## Summary

**Where you are now:** getting started. **What is enough for your risks:** three months of supplies. At your budget, the bare minimum (three days of water, light, warmth and medicine) is in place by month 4 (February 2027), and everything by month 25 (November 2028). Start with the free steps under Your plan.

### The three things that matter most

1. Of 100 households like yours, about 95 (70–100) will have to leave home quickly at least once in the next 10 years. Parts of your area flood in a hurricane's storm surge.[2] Know your evacuation zone and where you would go; leave when told.[3, 4] For chemical spills and releases, plan for as little as a few minutes of warning; for wildfires, 15 minutes.[5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11]
2. Of 100 households like yours, about 65 (60–85) will lose grid power for a day or more in the next 10 years. If you are not told to leave, be ready to manage about 7 days at home with no power, and about 1 month with no tap water.
3. Of 100 households like yours, about 60 (35–90) will be unable to shop for food and supplies for 3 days or more in the next 10 years. Keep about 2 weeks of food you normally eat, and 1½ months of daily medicine on hand.

**What the plan assumes you already have:** a charged mobile phone, go-bag for each person, manual can opener, a cooking pot with a lid, three days of the food you normally eat, a warm blanket for each person and warm layers for each person. If any is missing, untick "Assume everyday basics" on the Have screen and the plan will add it.

**Four ways to reach each other.** Emergency planners call this a PACE plan: a primary way, an alternate, a contingency and an emergency way. Each one takes over when the one before it fails.[13] For a household it can be:
