## Your risks

What could reach a household like yours in Cameron Parish, Louisiana over the next 10 years: the likeliest events, and the rarer ones that can kill, most likely first.

### What to know and do

#### 1. Medical emergency

Nearly every household like yours will have someone need emergency care in the next ten years.[15, 16]

**Includes:** far from emergency care; falls.

**What helps.** Take a first-aid and bleeding-control class. You may be able to save a life by acting right after an injury, before help arrives.[17] If a teen or adult collapses and their heart stops, call 911 and push hard and fast in the center of the chest. This hands-only CPR needs no training. Note where the nearest heart defibrillator (AED) is; it talks you through each step.[18] Keep a stocked first-aid kit. Check it regularly and replace anything used or out of date.[19] Keep a list of each person's medicines, doses and allergies with your emergency supplies.[20] Know how to reach 911. Call if you can, and text where that service works.[21]

**What to avoid.** Do not start antibiotics on your own or take someone else's. The wrong medicine can delay the right treatment and cause serious side effects.[22] Do not use expired medicines.[23]

**How bad:** Serious (based on data).

#### 2. Wildfire

Of 100 households like yours, about 88 (38 to nearly all) will have to leave home or lose power because of a wildfire in the next ten years.[6, 11]

**What helps.** Keep a zone at least 30 feet around your home clear of leaves, debris and anything that burns.[24] Know your evacuation zone and routes, and practice with your pets.[24] Store N95 masks for smoke. Pick a room you can close off from outside air, and run a portable air cleaner there.[24] N95 masks are not made to fit children, so for them the clean room is the protection.[25] A box fan with a MERV 13 filter makes a low-cost air cleaner.[26] If your heating and cooling system brings in fresh air, set it to recirculate.[24] Keep phones charged and have backup chargers.[24]

**What to avoid.** Leave as soon as authorities tell you to, even if you cannot see flames.[24] Do not use an air cleaner that makes ozone.[27] Avoid hard exercise when it is smoky, so you breathe in less smoke.[27]

**How bad:** Serious (rough data).

#### 3. Hurricane

Of 100 households like yours, about 78 (62–91) will lose power or have damage from a hurricane or tropical storm in the next ten years.[6, 7, 8, 10, 11]

**Includes:** inland flooding from a tropical storm.

**What helps.** Know your evacuation zone, your routes and where you would stay. If you live in a mandatory evacuation zone and officials tell you to leave, go right away.[4] If you are not told to leave, shelter from the wind in a small inside room, closet or hallway away from windows, on the lowest floor that will not flood.[4, 28] Clear drains and gutters, bring in outdoor furniture, and think about storm shutters. Keep phones charged and have backup chargers.[4] A flood policy typically takes up to 30 days to start, so buy it well before a storm.[29] If you would leave in an electric car, keep it fully charged all hurricane season.[30]

**What to avoid.** Never walk or drive through floodwater. One foot of moving water can sweep a car away.[29] Do not drive or charge an electric car that has been in floodwater. Salt water can start a battery fire.[30] Never run a generator inside your home or garage.[31]

**How bad:** Serious (mostly data).

#### 4. Lightning

Of 100 households like yours, about 15 (4–43) will have lightning damage their home or cut their power in the next ten years.[6, 11]

**What helps.** Pick your shelter spot now. A safe room or storm shelter is best.[32] The next best is a small, windowless room or basement on the lowest floor of a sturdy building.[32, 33] Sign up for your community's warnings, and learn what your sirens sound like.[32] Know the signs of a tornado: a rotating funnel cloud, a cloud of debris, or a roar like a freight train. In your shelter, protect your head and neck with your arms, and pile blankets or cushions around you.[32] When thunder roars, go indoors. Get into a building or a car with a roof.[34]

**What to avoid.** Stay away from windows, doors and outside walls.[32] There is no safe place in a car during a tornado, only less dangerous ones. If you are caught, stay buckled in and keep your head below the windows.[32] During a thunderstorm, avoid running water and electronics plugged into the wall.[34]

**How bad:** Very severe (rough data).

#### 5. Burst pipe or water leak

Of 100 households like yours, about 14 will have a burst pipe or leak flood part of the home in the next ten years.[35]

**Includes:** sewer backup.

**What helps.** Find your main water shut-off valve now, and show everyone how to turn it off. A burst pipe can flood a room quickly.[36, 37] Once a year, check the hoses to the water heater, washing machine, dishwasher and fridge, and replace any that crack or leak. A leak alarm can warn you early.[36] In freezing weather, let a faucet drip at night, open the cabinet doors under sinks on outside walls, and keep the heat at 55°F or higher.[37] Home and renters policies usually cover burst pipes. Many do not cover a sewer backup unless you add that cover, and floods need their own policy.[36]

**What to avoid.** Never thaw a frozen pipe with an open flame; use a hair dryer. Watch for electric shock around standing water.[37] Do not leave home while the washing machine or dishwasher is running.[36]

**How bad:** Severe (mostly data).

#### 6. Coastal flooding

Of 100 households like yours, about 9 will have coastal flooding reach their home in the next ten years.[5, 6]

**What helps.** Look up your address on FEMA's flood maps, and sign up for your community's warnings.[29] Homeowner's insurance does not cover flooding, and a flood policy typically takes up to 30 days to start.[29] Renters can buy flood coverage for their belongings.[38] Know how you would get to higher ground or a higher floor.[29]

**What to avoid.** Six inches of moving water can knock you down, and one foot can sweep your car away.[29] Never drive around barriers on a flooded road. The road may have collapsed under the water.[39] Stay off bridges over fast-moving water.[29] Leave if you are told to.[40]

**How bad:** Very severe (mostly data).

#### 7. House fire

Of 100 households like yours, about 3 will have a house fire in the next ten years.[41]

**Includes:** carbon monoxide poisoning; lithium battery fire.

**What helps.** Put smoke alarms inside and outside every bedroom and on every level, and test them each month.[42] Practice your escape plan twice a year, including finding your way out in the dark.[43] Sleep with bedroom doors closed. Teach children not to hide from firefighters.[43] If there is smoke, crawl low under it to your exit.[43] If you cannot get out, close the door, cover vents and cracks with cloth or tape, call 911, and signal from the window with a light-colored cloth or a flashlight.[43] Insurance and copies of your documents help you recover afterward.[44]

**What to avoid.** Before you open a door, feel the door and the knob. If either is hot, or smoke is coming around it, keep it closed and use your second way out.[43] If a person or pet is still inside, get out and tell firefighters right away.[43] If your clothes catch fire, stop, drop and roll.[43]

**How bad:** Severe (based on data).

#### 8. Tornado

Of 100 households like yours, about 2 (1–6) will have a tornado damage or cut off their neighborhood in the next ten years.[6, 11]

**What helps.** The steps under "Lightning" above apply here too.

**How bad:** Very severe (rough data).

- Heat and cold waves are marked Serious for this household because someone in it is 65 or older; they are most dangerous for households like yours.
- Wildfire smoke is marked Serious for this household because someone in it is 65 or older; smoke harms them most.

## Your targets

How long to be ready for each kind of disruption at the 1-in-100 setting. At this setting, about 1 in 10 households like yours will face a longer disruption of any one kind in the next 10 years; about 2 in 10 will face at least one kind that runs past its target. That is why the plan also gives you ways to cope when a target runs out.[11, 89]

| If this happens | Be ready for | Help likely in | Mostly back in | Enough at |

| No grid power at home | about 7 days (up to 10 days) | about 3 days | about 16 days | two weeks |
| Tap water must be treated | not needed at this setting | not known | not known | free steps |
| No tap water at all | about 1 month (3 weeks to 1½ months) | about 3 days | about 1 month | one month |
| Can't get to a store | about 2 weeks (10 days to 1 month) | not known | not known | two weeks |
| Dangerous heat or cold indoors | about 5 days (up to 7 days) | about 3 days | about 6 days | two weeks |
| Medication and medical-supply continuity | about 1½ months (1–3) | not known | not known | three months |
| No phone, internet or card payments | about 5 days (3–10) | not known | not known | two weeks |

Brackets show how uncertain a target is. "Not known": no restoration records for the event behind that target.

**How well do these numbers hold up?** Tested against 22 real disasters, this version covered 6, partly covered 9, fell short on 6 and could not model 1.[90] Treat each target as a floor, not a promise. If your area has lived through something longer, plan for that.

### No grid power at home: about 7 days (up to 10 days)

**What helps.** A light for each person, a radio and phone power are in your plan; keeping food cold and charging up are on the forecast list; registries are under Local help.

**What to avoid.** Never run a generator inside your home or garage, even with the doors and windows open. Keep it outside, more than 20 feet from windows, doors and vents.[31] Put a carbon monoxide alarm on every level of your home.[91] Headache, dizziness, nausea or confusion can mean carbon monoxide poisoning. Get everyone outside to fresh air, then call 911.[92] Never heat your home with a gas stove or oven. Unplug electronics, because the power can come back with a surge that damages them.[91] Treat every downed power line as live: stay at least 30 feet from it and anything it touches, and call 911.[93] If one falls on your car, stay inside unless the car is on fire.[94]

The worst power cut in your region's records (where it was worst, about 55 miles (88 km) away) was Hurricane Laura (2020); being ready for a week would have left some homes that lost power still waiting (about 60 in 100 of all customers there were still out).[5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 95, 96]

### No tap water at all: about 1 month (3 weeks to 1½ months)

**What helps.** Store at least one gallon per person per day, for drinking and keeping clean.[1] Fill clean bottles or jugs with tap water and replace it every six months.[97] You can pick a level in the plan. About 3 liters a day covers drinking to survive, one gallon is the basic default, and about 4 gallons (15 liters) is the humanitarian minimum for drinking, cooking and washing.[98] A tank water heater holds 20 to 80 gallons of clean water.[99, 100] For long outages, a filter and a source of raw water go further than more jugs.[89] Filters do not remove viruses, so add a disinfectant such as chlorine dioxide after filtering.[101] A two-bucket toilet keeps waste safe when toilets cannot flush.[102]

**What to avoid.** Do not store water in containers that held chemicals.[97] Milk jugs seal poorly and turn brittle.[103] Never drink pool or spa water. Use it only for washing and cleaning.[100] After a flood, do not drink from a private well until it has been disinfected and tested. Your health department can tell you how.[104]

### Can't get to a store: about 2 weeks (10 days to 1 month)

**What helps.** The food is on your checklists, counted in calories, not servings: pick foods you already eat, and use the oldest first.

**What to avoid.** Do not buy everything at once. It strains your budget and the store. Do not buy or eat from cans that bulge, leak, are rusted or are deeply dented.[105] Do not trust a kit's "days" label. Check the calories on the package instead.

This rounds up to 2 weeks: before rounding it is about 2 weeks, just past 10 days.[6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 51, 52, 57, 58, 106, 107]

### Dangerous heat or cold indoors: about 5 days (up to 7 days)

**What helps.** Agree who checks on whom, especially older neighbours and anyone who lives alone.[108, 109] In heat, go where there is air conditioning. Dial 2-1-1 to find one.[108] Cover windows with drapes or shades.[110] In cold, close off rooms you don't need, stuff towels under doors, and cover windows with blankets at night. Have extra blankets, sleeping bags and warm coats.[109] Babies under one year old should never sleep in a cold room.[109] If you cannot keep your home warm, go to a warming center. Dial 2-1-1 to find one.[111] If you heat with wood, have the stove and chimney professionally inspected and cleaned every year, because creosote from the smoke builds up and can start a fire.[112]

**What to avoid.** Fans move air but do not lower body temperature.[110] Above 90°F indoors, a fan can make you hotter.[108] Never heat your home with a gas oven, and never use a grill or camp stove indoors.[31] Headache, dizziness, nausea or confusion can mean carbon monoxide poisoning: get outside, then call 911.[92] Keep space heaters 3 feet from anything that can burn.[113] Never leave people or pets in a closed car on a warm day.[110]

### Medication and medical-supply continuity: about 1½ months (1–3)

**What helps.** See Medicine under Special needs.

**What to avoid.** Do not throw insulin away after a day without power. If it gets hotter than 86°F and you have nothing else, use it, and replace it as soon as you can.[114] Never use insulin that has frozen or looks unusual, with particles, clumps, crystals or a changed color.[114, 115] Do not use expired medicines. Weak antibiotics can fail to treat an infection.[23] Do not share antibiotics or save them for later.[22]

This rounds up to 6 weeks: before rounding it is about 4 weeks, just past a month.[6, 7, 9, 11, 41, 49, 50, 57, 58, 116]

### No phone, internet or card payments: about 5 days (3–10)

**What helps.** See Your family plan (staying in touch), the wallet cards and the list for when a storm is forecast.

**What to avoid.** Do not rely on one source of news. Do not assume you can text 911 everywhere. It is not available in every area, so call 911 if you can.[21]

This rounds up to 5 days: before rounding it is about 3.4 days, just past 3 days.[6, 7, 8, 10, 11, 45]

**What helps.** See Your family plan and Your shelter plan.

**What to avoid.** Many people wait to check with others before they act on a warning.[117] Always follow the instructions of local officials, and leave early enough to avoid being trapped by bad weather.[3] Never walk or drive through floodwater. Six inches of moving water can knock you down.[29]

**What helps.** See Your family plan and Your shelter plan.

**What to avoid.** Do not force down water when you are not thirsty. Too much water can be harmful.[118] In heat, do not drink more than 6 cups an hour.[119] If you are stuck in a car in a snowstorm, staying in the car is often safest. Run the engine about 10 minutes an hour with a window cracked, and keep the exhaust pipe clear of snow.[109]

**What helps.** See "Medical emergency" under Your risks.

### House fire

**What helps.** See "House fire" under Your risks and the safety rules under Your plan.

**What to avoid.** If a person or pet is still inside, get out, call 911, and tell firefighters where they are.[43] Never heat your home with an oven.[113] Turn off space heaters when you leave the room or go to bed.[113] Replace 9-volt alarm batteries at least once a year.[42] If you smell gas or hear hissing, get everyone out without touching switches or phones, then call 911 and the gas company from a safe distance.[120, 121] Only a professional should turn the gas back on.[121]

**What helps.** See the home-security and trusted-circle steps in Your plan.

**What to avoid.** After a disaster, be careful with people who show up offering fast repairs or help for a fee. Report scams at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.[122] Do not hide a spare key under the doormat or a planter. Leave it with a trusted neighbour.[123]

**What helps.** See the clean room under Your shelter plan.

**What to avoid.** Do not use an air cleaner that makes ozone.[124] While the air is bad, avoid frying, candles, smoking and vacuuming without a HEPA filter, and skip hard exercise.[27] Masks with ear loops or one strap do not seal, so they will not protect your lungs.[125] If you have heart or lung disease or are pregnant, ask your doctor before wearing a respirator.[125]

## Your shelter plan

Pick a spot for each danger below, at home and at work, and practice going there.[12]

**Strong wind.** In a high wind or severe thunderstorm warning, go inside a sturdy building, to an inside room or basement.[133] Stay away from windows while damaging wind is near.[134]

**Tornado.** A safe room or storm shelter is best; next is a small inside room with no windows on the lowest floor.[32] Even a tied-down mobile home is not safe.[33]

**Hurricane.** If officials tell your evacuation zone to leave, go right away. If you stay, use an inside room away from windows.[4]

**Chemical release.** If told to stay inside, go to an above-ground room with few openings. Close the windows, doors and vents, turn off fans and air conditioning, and seal the room with plastic sheeting and duct tape.[135]

**Smoke.** Make one room a clean room: close its windows and doors, and run an air cleaner that does not make ozone.[124]

**Radiation.** If officials warn of fallout, get inside, stay inside, stay tuned. Go to a basement or the middle of a brick or concrete building.[86]

## When a storm, freeze or heat wave is forecast

Hurricanes, winter storms and heat waves usually come with warning. Keep your phone charged when one is forecast, and use the time the same way each time.[4]

**Before any storm**

- Charge phones, power banks and other batteries.[136] 
- Fill the car's tank and get some cash, since card readers and cash machines need power.[136] Charge the power station.[136] If you would leave in an electric car, charge it fully.[30]
- Refill prescriptions if you can.[136]
- Fill the bathtub and other large containers with water for flushing and cleaning.[136]
- Turn the fridge to its coldest setting and keep the doors shut.[136] A full freezer keeps food cold for about 48 hours, a fridge for about four.[91]
- Bring in or tie down outdoor furniture and grills.[4]
- Check your evacuation zone and your plan to leave.[4]
- Check with neighbors, older adults and anyone who may need help.[4]

**Before a hard freeze.** Let hot and cold water drip from a faucet at night, open the cabinet doors under sinks on outside walls, and keep the heat at 55°F or higher. Make sure everyone knows how to shut off the water in case a pipe bursts.[37]

**Before a heat wave.** Pick a place to cool down, such as a library, or ask your local health department about cooling options. Plan to check on family, older adults and neighbors. Fans do not lower body temperature.[110]

## After a disaster: the first 30 days

**Your county.** Cameron Parish, Louisiana had 3 federal major-disaster declarations in the last five full years.[159]

Recovery takes weeks. These steps come in rough order.

**Going home.** Go back only when local officials say it is safe. Do not go inside if you smell gas or the building looks damaged.[160] Run a generator only outside, more than 20 feet from windows, doors and vents.[31]

**Insurance and records.** Before you clean up, take photos and videos and make a list of the damage.[160] Keep every receipt.[161] Call your insurer as soon as you can, and an adjuster will come to inspect. Check the adjuster's estimate, and talk to them before you sign a repair contract.[162]

**Help from FEMA.** If a federal disaster declaration covers your county, apply at DisasterAssistance.gov or call 1-800-621-3362.[163] FEMA help does not replace insurance.[164]

**Scams.** FEMA never charges to apply or to inspect.[165] Its inspectors carry an official photo ID and never ask for your bank details; a FEMA shirt is not an ID.[161] Never sign your insurance check over to a contractor, and walk away from anyone who wants cash up front.[166]

**Medicine.** In a declared disaster, Medicare drug plans can help you find a pharmacy and replace lost medicine.[167] Many states let a pharmacist give an emergency supply when your prescriber cannot be reached, and the rules differ by state.[147] Healthcare Ready's Rx Open map shows which pharmacies are open in a disaster area.[168]

**Papers.** To replace lost IDs, start with your birth certificate, from the vital records office of the state where you were born.[169]

**How likely here.** From your own power curve, power out for two months or more: between 1 in 3,000 and 1 in 660 households like yours in the next 10 years; for three months or more: between 1 in 13,000 and 1 in 2,400.[5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 95, 96]

These pointers are for the rare event that lasts for months. They are places to start, not a manual.

**Rain.** Each state sets its own rules on collecting rain, and the rules vary widely, so check yours.[170] Rainwater is not safe to drink until germs and chemicals are removed, but it can water plants you do not eat.[171]

**Wells.** A well pump stops when the power goes out. Have a licensed electrician connect any generator.[172] A hand pump fitted to the well can still draw water in a long outage; test and treat that water before drinking it.[173]

**Toilets.** After a strong earthquake, toilets may not flush for weeks or months. A twin-bucket toilet keeps pee and poo apart, and handling poo safely stops diseases like cholera.[102]

**Food.** Badly home-canned food can cause botulism. Vegetables, meat and fish need a pressure canner.[174] Use tested recipes, such as those from the National Center for Home Food Preservation.[175] Your state or county Extension service can help with growing and preserving food.[174]

**Spirits.** Keep regular sleep and wake times, take breaks from the news, and talk with people you trust.[176] Keep books, games and puzzles for children.[140]
